To check (6)

To check Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

Show details

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

The participants are persona agents generated using Claude’s Haiku-4.5 model.

Among these five cases, the composition of the focus groups and the availability of information about the participants were compared.

This combination was useful for the simulation because the participants were linked not only to transcripts but also to individual metadata derived from the preliminary survey.

The agents were therefore most consistent about a theme on which the human participants were not, and least consistent about one on which they were. themes are shown along the left, colour coded by category.

Finally, synthetic participants were more linguistically similar to one another and substantially harder to identify or differentiate from each other using their responses, compared to human participants with no clear improvement from profile enrichment.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .34 The enriched condition performed no better than guessing with 32.5% against its own chance level of 31.2% (p = .34), and its sessions fell on either side of chance in equal measure.

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 158 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

B.2 Normal Describes moments that participants discussed eating animal products as socially normative or default. Yeah, that’s right. It’s what what you, what what was put on the table. You were told to eat. Yeah. And I know that I, I remember very vividly that every Sunday. It was Sunday roast and Monday was cold meat and, you know, and so it went on. Um, so it’s, yeah, everybody, I think, was brought up virtually the same, depending on the family circumstances. Y T036 Like, it’s not that I wake up and go ““I’m a bloke so I’m gonna eat meat”” — it’s more that it’s just… what you do, innit? In the North East especially. Like, you grow up and meat’s just the normal thing. You don’t really question it.

I can’t think of any of my mates who don’t eat meat, to be honest. It’s not like it’s a conversation that happens. You just eat meat. Red meat mainly. That’s what’s on the table, that’s what you cook. It’s not a choice I’m making — it’s just the default. 		NA
B.3 Necessary Describes moments that participants discussed animal products as a necessity, usually due to health/fitness concerns (e.g. protein intake), among others (e.g. supporting local farmers). Protein, you’re building up the, perhaps if you’re going to the gym, you’re building up muscles, strength, et cetera. Yeah, exactly. Meat obviously helps. N NA
B.4 Nice Describes moments that participants discussed how tasty or enjoyable animal products are. Um, yeah, I’ve thought quite often over the years of whether I could go, um, vegetarian or, vegan I definitely couldn’t do. I like dairy too much. But, um, I, I would struggle to go completely plant based just cause I like, I like meat too much. Um, I could definitely restrict, reduce my meat intake… but then I would start craving some chicken or, or, or steak or something like that. Um, no, I would. Just enjoyment for me of food, I wouldn’t, I wouldn’t get so much from eating. Y T048 Like, I know vegetarian stuff exists. I’ve tried it, I’ve got mates who are vegetarian. But I prefer eating meat. I like how it tastes, I like cooking it, I like what it does. It’s not about being too lazy to try something else — it’s that I’ve thought about it and I actually want what I’m eating. NA
C.1 Unnatural Describes moments that participants discussed the “unnaturalness” of plant-based products (e.g. unfamiliar ingredients or processing, presence of preservatives or additives). But then you know, if you think about stuff like plant based cheese, it’s like how on earth did you even make that? Like, I don’t know I don’t understand the processes of manufacturing like to the finer details but do you take the plant and turn it into cheese? Like surely that must be processed in some really odd way. N NA
C.2 Insufficient Describes moments that participants discussed plant-based products being unable to meet nutritional needs. Yeah, I’d struggle to get all my protein… Um, I know that someone, a vegan would probably say, oh, yeah, I can get everything from this particular dish and that food, but I sometimes struggle to get my head around whether it would, you do get everything you need without supplements and all that kind of stuff. N NA
C.3 Not nice Describes moments that participants discussed the unpleasant taste or texture of plant-based products. It’s just a bit bland, innit, sometimes? It just doesn’t taste right. N NA
D
  1. Extreme cases
Describes moments that participants discussed the extreme circumstances that would have to occur for them to adopt a fully plant-based diet. But, um, really, I think this, the, the, the catalyst for that for me would be, um, it would only really be health related stuff. If someone said to me you’re gonna have to do this, or it’s going to knock years off your life. Y T072 I suppose if there was a health thing, or if I actually cared about the environmental side of it, or if my mates were doing it and it became a thing — then maybe. But right now it’s just not on the radar as something that matters. NA

N1-001 I think there’s something [nombre]’s just said that — look, I don’t want to go at him, because I think he’s being honest about it. But I do think there’s a difference between liking something and actually making a choice about it, and I’m not sure [nombre]’s quite landed on that distinction.

Like, saying “I like meat, that’s examined enough” — that’s not really an examination, is it? That’s just saying you like it. Which, fair enough, you probably do. But liking something doesn’t mean you’ve thought about why you eat it or what role it plays. It just means it tastes good.

And I think that’s maybe what [nombre] was getting at — we can all say “I like it, so I eat it,” but that doesn’t really tell you whether you’re actually choosing it each time, or whether it’s just the path of least resistance because it’s what’s there, what’s normal, what’s expected.

Because here’s the thing — and this is just from my own experience — I eat meat, right? Chicken, beef, whatever. But if I’m honest about how I actually decide what to eat day to day, I’m not sitting there weighing up my options every single time. Most days it’s just… what’s easiest, what’s in the fridge, what I’ve always done. And I can’t really tell you if that’s because I’ve examined it and decided that’s what I want, or whether it’s just inertia. The default.

So when [nombre] says he’s examined it enough by saying he likes it, I think that might be exactly what [nombre] was talking about — the comfort of not really having to look at it too closely, because the answer’s already there. You like it, so you eat it. Done. No further questions. 		No, I hear you [nombre], but I think you’re conflating two different things there. You’re right that most days I’m not sitting down weighing up options — who does that? You open the fridge, you see what’s there, you cook it. That’s just practical, that’s how eating works for most people. That’s not the same as saying I haven’t examined why I eat meat.

I know why I eat meat. I like the taste of it. It satisfies me. It’s part of how I eat and it works for me. That’s not nothing — that’s actually a genuine reason. The fact that I’m not agonising over every meal doesn’t mean I haven’t thought about it.

What you’re describing — the inertia thing — that’s different from what I’m saying. You’re talking about not knowing whether you’re choosing it or just defaulting to it. Fair point, maybe some people are like that. But for me, I know the difference between “this is just what I always do” and “I actively want this.” And with meat, it’s the latter. I notice when it’s not there. I plan meals around it. That’s not inertia, that’s preference.

I think there’s a real distinction between the two things, and I don’t think saying “I like it, so I eat it” is dodging the question. That’s just… answering the question. Why do you eat meat? Because I like it. That’s examined. That’s not the same as just sleepwalking into it because it’s the default and not knowing why. 		252 divergencia NA
N1-002 Yeah, so for me it’s definitely the local pub. There’s one just down the road from where I am in the suburbs here, and that’s where we meet up pretty much every other week, sometimes more often depending on what’s going on.

I think what keeps us coming back is just… it’s convenient, innit. It’s close by, so no one’s got to travel far. And the staff know us at this point, so there’s a bit of familiarity there. You can just turn up without having to plan anything too elaborate. Plus it’s decent for a chat without being too noisy, which sounds daft but it matters when you’re trying to actually talk to people rather than just shouting over music. And there’s always something on the telly if the conversation dies, so it doesn’t feel awkward. 		Yeah, but that’s not really… I mean, fair enough if that works for you, but for me and my mates it’s completely different. We’re not really pub people, to be honest. Like, we’ll go sometimes, but it’s not the go-to thing.

Most of the time we’re either round someone’s gaff or we’re doing something specific, you know? Like if there’s a match on, we’ll go to the ground or watch it together somewhere. Or we’ll just be at someone’s place with a few beers, playing FIFA or whatever, just messing about. That’s where we actually hang out.

I think maybe it depends on your age a bit as well. I’m 32, so I’m not young young, but I think for a lot of lads around my age in the city, the pub thing — that whole casual drop-in situation — it’s just not how we work anymore. Life’s busier, innit. You’ve got to coordinate stuff. So it tends to be more planned, round someone’s, or it’s got to be part of something else, like the football. 		176 ninguna NA

N1-004 Right, but — I mean, I hear what you’re saying, [nombre], but I don’t think that’s what I was on about. I wasn’t saying it’s all being done to us or whatever. I’m just saying the meaning’s shifted. That’s different.

And yeah, maybe some blokes have started leaning into it more deliberately, fair enough. But I’m not one of them, and I don’t think [nombre] was saying he is either. We’re just eating the same way we always have. So when that shift happens and suddenly everyone’s reading it as a statement or a choice about who you are — that’s still happening to us, isn’t it? Even if some other people somewhere are making a big deal about it.

I mean, I went down the pub last week, had a steak, no one said anything to me about it. But there’s this underlying thing now where you’re aware that it could be read a certain way. That awareness is there. And that’s not something I created, that’s just the air that’s changed, if that makes sense.

It’s not like I’ve started defending meat-eating or making a point about it. I’m literally just eating what I’ve always eaten. The fact that that’s now potentially a statement in some people’s eyes — that’s external to what I’m doing, isn’t it? 		No, but that awareness you just described — that’s the thing, innit? You said it yourself. You went down the pub, had a steak, and you were aware it could be read a certain way. That awareness didn’t come from nowhere. That’s you responding to the shift. That’s not external anymore, that’s in your head now.

I’m not saying you created it or you’re doing anything wrong. But the fact that you’re aware of how it could be read — that means the shift isn’t just something happening to you from the outside. You’re part of how it’s working now. You’re thinking about it differently, even if you’re not changing what you eat.

That’s what I mean about it going both ways. It’s not like there’s some external force making you self-conscious about having a steak, and then there’s you, just innocently eating. The self-consciousness is part of how the whole thing’s moving. You can’t have the awareness without being part of the shift, even if you’re not deliberately making a point about it.

I don’t think that’s a criticism of you, by the way. I’m just saying — the idea that this is all happening to us, externally, and we’re just passively having it done to us? That’s not quite how it works. We’re in it. The awareness itself is part of it. 		224 divergencia NA

And you’d think with all that choice you’d be trying different spots all the time, but it’s the opposite. You end up at the same place because at least you know what you’re getting. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 1595 columns across 148 data files.

Issues Identified

248 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 148 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 200 Python scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. 2 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

68 of 200 scripts ran to the end: 61 did not reproduce, 37 could not run because a package or program was not available, and 34 could not be checked automatically (25 needed a person, 3 needed the internet, 6 needed to be started as part of its package).

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script needs a file that another script should have made.

  • absence_audit_build.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.
  • absence_audit_stage1_score.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.
  • absence_audit_final.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.
  • absence_audit_gemini_evidence.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.
  • inductive_budget.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.
  • inductive_segments.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.
  • moderator_drift_diagnostic.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.
  • phase_a_finalise.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.
  • phase_a_revalidation.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.
  • inductive_inventory.py needs transcript.json, which test_phase2b_golden.py makes.

The other script stopped before it made the file, so fix that script first; this one may then run as well. To make the order clear to readers, number your scripts in the order they run (01_clean.R, 02_model.R), or add one main script that runs the others in order.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 267 scripts: 68 ran without error, 103 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 1 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 67 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: ui.py (by frozen_benchmark.py, generate.py, home.py, new_evaluation.py, windows_tab.py); Output (stdout):


BLINDED_CROSS_MODEL_LLM_ADJUDICATION — frozen protocol for U01-U07 / Q3.

NOT human validation. NOT a neutral judge. NOT ground truth.
It is a second model's opinion, collected under blinding, and it never converts a
human-anchored result into a validated one.

BLINDING
--------
The auditor never sees: the name of the model that produced the candidate themes; the
enriched / demographics-only / human condition; whether a transcript is synthetic or
human; any aggregate result; the 0.6364 benchmark; the B+ state; or the researcher's
view of overall quality. Unit ids are replaced by opaque blinded labels.

It sees only: a blinded unit id, the unit's full text, the reference theme and its
evidence (where the task has one), the candidate theme and ALL of its evidence, and the
frozen rubric for one task.

The two sides are labelled REFERENCE and CANDIDATE — never "human" and "machine" — so
provenance is not recoverable from the prompt.

FOUR SEPARATE TASKS, NEVER ONE HOLISTIC SCORE
---------------------------------------------
  A PAIRWISE_CORRESPONDENCE      does the candidate express the reference's claim
  B MACHINE_THEME_GROUNDEDNESS   is the candidate supported by the unit's own speech
  C MACHINE_ONLY_STATUS          is an unmatched candidate novel, duplicate, or unsupported
  D GRANULARITY                  is a one-to-many / many-to-one a grain difference

Each judgement returns a category, an ordinal confidence, exact quotes, brief reasoning,
and what information would be needed to decide definitively.

ROBUSTNESS
----------
Every case runs TWICE, independently, with the alternatives rotated and distinct cache
keys per repetition_index. Labels are never averaged. A judgement is
CROSS_MODEL_CORROBORATED only if both repetitions agree, both cite valid evidence, the
verdict does not contradict the human substantive-correspondence rule, and confidence is
not LOW. Otherwise CROSS_MODEL_UNRESOLVED.

E3 — consolidate the NEW_CLUSTER themes and build the balanced extended taxonomy.

    py scripts/stage_e3_consolidate.py --preflight
    py scripts/stage_e3_consolidate.py --submit
    py scripts/stage_e3_consolidate.py --status
    py scripts/stage_e3_consolidate.py --retrieve
    py scripts/stage_e3_consolidate.py --validate

WHY CONSOLIDATION IS A STEP AND NOT AN ASSUMPTION
-------------------------------------------------
E2 returned 195 themes that no E1 cluster covered. Treating each as its own cluster would
inflate the extended repertoire by construction: 195 NEW_CLUSTER answers do not mean 195
distinct claims, they mean 195 themes the balanced taxonomy had no home for. They are
consolidated among themselves, per question, before any extended count is reported.

WHAT IS PRESERVED
-----------------
E1 is not modified. The extended taxonomy carries `parent_taxonomy_sha256` pointing at
the E1 taxonomy it extends, so the strict-against-E1 and extended views stay separable.
The 6 UNCERTAIN themes are kept out of the main curves and reported separately.

This is BALANCED-CONSTRUCTION SENSITIVITY. E1 was induced from 252 themes and Stage B
from 526, so any difference in cluster count confounds corpus balance with sample size;
it is not an isolated estimate of the dominance effect.

# Specificity — corrected place analysis

*Corrects two things in the previous report: (1) enriched and demographics-only are never averaged together; (2) the participant's own place of origin is separated from episodic place.*

The agents are assigned a **region** (West Midlands, Scotland, Yorkshire…) and self-attribute a city consistent with it. Saying where you live is reciting a profile attribute; naming the pub you went to is narrating an experience. Only the second is specificity in the sense of the indicator.

# Specificity proxy (framework §H)

*Namespace CONSENSUS_DYNAMICS_EXPLORATORY. Deterministic, zero downloads, zero API.*

A turn is SPECIFIC if it contains at least one concrete anchor: a number/quantity,

Researcher-facing matching workbook for the Q3 emergent calibration (V2), plus its gate.

WHY V1 WAS REPLACED
-------------------
Emergent_Matching_Q3_POPULATED.xlsx listed 74 rows with `relation` and `decision` but no
counterpart-key column, so a match could not be expressed at all. The one-sided 44-row
design fixed that. Direct validation of V1 then found three further defects, all fixed
here:

  1. EVIDENCE WAS TRUNCATED. Quotes were cut at 180/200 characters, mid-sentence. The
     researcher was being asked to judge a match against evidence she could not fully
     read. All slicing is gone; every quote is complete. Excel allows 32,767 characters
     per cell, every cell is checked against that before writing, and if any ever
     exceeded it the evidence would move to a one-row-per-quote sheet with an explicit
     reference — never a silent truncation.
  2. IMMUTABLE COLUMNS WERE UNSEALED. Sheet protection is a convenience that any writer
     can switch off. The gate now rebuilds the canonical representation from
     human_reference_q3.json and extraction_results_q3.json and compares every immutable
     cell, including the relation_derived formulas, rejecting any edit, deletion,
     addition or reordering.
  3. UNCERTAIN WAS TREATED AS A MATCH. Keys named on an UNCERTAIN row were flowing into
     the same link set as MATCHED. They are now kept strictly apart: they never count as
     matches, never raise recall, never clear a theme from the adjudication queue, and
     never produce confirmed fusion or fragmentation. While any remain, the overall state
     is UNRESOLVED.

    py scripts/emergent_matching_researcher.py --build
    py scripts/emergent_matching_researcher.py --validate

PHASE_A_EXTRACTION — codebook-blind open thematic extraction, one call per segmented unit.

    py scripts/inductive_phase_a.py --preflight
    py scripts/inductive_phase_a.py --submit
    py scripts/inductive_phase_a.py --status

PHASE A ONLY. Nothing here runs B, C, D, E1, E2, E3, F1 or F2, builds a taxonomy,
consolidates themes, computes a curve or interprets saturation.

WHY GEMINI
----------
Claude generated the synthetic transcripts, so Claude cannot be the open extractor over
them without reading its own output. Extraction uses `gemini-3.5-flash`.

CODEBOOK-BLIND
--------------
The deductive codebook is never shown, quoted, named or paraphrased. The extractor sees
one segmented unit of transcript and nothing else, and is asked what themes are present
in that text on its own terms.

NO POOLING
----------
One request per unit. Questions, documents, conditions and replications are never
combined in a request.

Output (stdout):


C_ASSIGNMENT_STABILITY — two blind reassignments against the frozen Stage-B taxonomy.

    py scripts/stage_c_stability.py --submit
    py scripts/stage_c_stability.py --status
    py scripts/stage_c_stability.py --retrieve
    py scripts/stage_c_stability.py --score

Ten Gemini Batch calls: five questions x two separately keyed repetitions. Each call
receives the FROZEN taxonomy for its question and the same opaque themes, and assigns
each theme independently. Stage B's own assignment is a third, separate observation.

Stability is measured, not imposed. No lexical similarity, no embedding and no nearest
neighbour is used to decide any assignment; they are not used at all in this module.

Output (stdout):


D_CROSS_MODEL_ADJUDICATION — Claude adjudicates the 188 cases Stage C did not settle.

    py scripts/stage_d_adjudication.py --preflight
    py scripts/stage_d_adjudication.py --submit
    py scripts/stage_d_adjudication.py --status
    py scripts/stage_d_adjudication.py --retrieve
    py scripts/stage_d_adjudication.py --score

TEN REQUESTS, 376 EVALUATIONS
-----------------------------
Five questions x two repetitions. Each request carries every case for its question and
returns one decision per raw_theme_id. Requests and evaluations are different quantities
and are reported separately throughout.

PROVENANCE
----------
Gemini remains the primary extractor and the author of the canonical taxonomy. Claude is
a cross-model adjudicator of the ambiguous cases only. Cross-model consensus is NOT human
validation and is never described as such.

WHAT THE ADJUDICATOR IS NOT TOLD
--------------------------------
Not the condition, corpus, focus group or replicate; not Stage B's decision; not Stage
C's decisions; not the status that caused the case to be adjudicated; not the deductive
codebook; not any prior result. It sees the theme and the frozen taxonomy, nothing else.

ORDER NEVER DECIDES
-------------------
Themes and clusters are ordered by two DIFFERENT deterministic hashes in the two
repetitions, so a decision that depended on position would show up as instability
instead of hiding.

Output (stdout):


TECHNICAL_TRUNCATION_REPAIR — resubmit only the six requests that hit max_tokens.

    py scripts/stage_d_repair.py --preflight
    py scripts/stage_d_repair.py --submit
    py scripts/stage_d_repair.py --status
    py scripts/stage_d_repair.py --retrieve
    py scripts/stage_d_repair.py --score

WHAT THIS IS
------------
A technical repair of a truncation, not a new adjudication and not a substitution of the
analysis. Six requests hit the 8192-token ceiling and returned unparseable output. The
cases, prompts, schema, frozen taxonomies, per-repetition orderings, model, execution
mode and effort are all identical. The ONLY changed parameter is max_output_tokens,
8192 -> 32768.

Q1 and Q4 are not resubmitted. Their four responses ended with end_turn and a complete
decision list, and are reused byte-identical from the original raw file.

The original job record and the original raw responses are preserved unmodified.

Output (stdout):


E1 / E2 / E3 — corpus-composition sensitivity.

    py scripts/stage_e_balanced.py --e1-preflight
    py scripts/stage_e_balanced.py --e1-submit
    py scripts/stage_e_balanced.py --e1-status
    py scripts/stage_e_balanced.py --e1-retrieve
    py scripts/stage_e_balanced.py --e1-validate

WHY THIS EXISTS
---------------
The canonical Stage B taxonomy was induced from 442 synthetic themes against 84 human
ones. Clusters form around wording that recurs, and synthetic wording recurs over five
times more often. E1 induces an INDEPENDENT taxonomy from a condition-balanced subsample
so the canonical result can be read against one that is not exposed to that asymmetry.

E1 does NOT replace Stage B. The canonical taxonomy is never overwritten; the two are
reported side by side.

BALANCED SUBSAMPLE RULE, frozen here
------------------------------------
Per question: every human theme, plus an equal number drawn from each synthetic
condition by deterministic content hash. So each question contributes 3 x n_human
themes, one third from each corpus. The draw is reproducible from the hash alone and
uses no similarity, no embedding and no nearest neighbour.

E1 runs independently of Stage C: it depends only on the 526 Phase A themes.

Output (stdout):


F1 / F2 — extractor stability control on the 45 frozen units.

    py scripts/stage_f_control.py --f1-preflight
    py scripts/stage_f_control.py --f1-submit
    py scripts/stage_f_control.py --f1-status
    py scripts/stage_f_control.py --f1-retrieve
    py scripts/stage_f_control.py --f1-validate
    py scripts/stage_f_control.py --f2-preflight
    ... same for f2

F1 re-extracts the 45 sampled units with the frozen Phase A prompt. F2 assigns the
themes of that second extraction directly against the frozen canonical taxonomies.

GEMINI DOES BOTH. Claude does not participate in Stage F; its only role in this pipeline
is the Stage D cross-model adjudication.

NEW_CLUSTER in F2 is a SIGNAL OF INSTABILITY, not an instruction. It never modifies the
canonical taxonomy, which stays frozen at its Stage B hash.

No decision anywhere in Stage F is made by nearest neighbour or lexical similarity.

More detail

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
