Methods

For this study, a custom system was developed to generate synthetic focus groups, in order to maintain control and traceability over the elements that make up the simulation. The architecture allows persona agents to converse following real discussion guides presented by a moderator agent within a structure that approximates some basic features of focus group dynamics, including speaking turns not being predefined and the moderator being able to adapt the guide according to the flow of the discussion. Its ultimate function was to produce focus groups in text form and generate synthetic transcripts comparable to human ones.

The system is organized into three main roles: participants, moderator, and orchestrator (see Figure 1). The participants are persona agents generated using Claude's Haiku-4.5 model. Each persona agent corresponds to a specific participant in the original human focus group and is constructed from the participant-level information available for that person in the source dataset. The selected information is stored in an individual JSON file, which serves as a structured participant profile, allowing all agents to be created using the same format. Just before an agent intervenes, the system converts this profile into a natural-language description so that the model can respond based on that profile. For example, one of the participants might be presented to the model as follows: "You are John, a 33-year-old male participant in a focus group.

You live in an urban area in Scotland, UK. Your typical eating patterns -speak from these naturally; do not list them, just let them inform your answers -include: red meat once a week..."

The moderator, generated using Claude's Sonnet-4.6 model, leads the session by following the discussion guide, but without mechanically repeating it. At each turn, the moderator first decides whether to intervene or let the conversation continue among the participants. If the moderator intervenes, they can choose from actions such as delving deeper into a topic, addressing a specific participant, or moving on to the next section. This decision is made within a set of actions defined in the system (see Appendix B), although the content of each intervention is generated by the model. That set of actions is based on the functions that the literature attributes to a human moderator: clarifying and regulating the discussion, supporting the generation of information, and facilitating interaction (Acocella & Cataldi, 2021).

Lastly, the orchestrator is not an agent, nor does it make its own calls to the model; rather, it is an internal layer of code. Its function is to handle the administrative aspects of the session so that the moderator can focus on leading the discussion, while the orchestrator maintains the operational continuity of the session. Specifically, the orchestrator compiles the transcript from the moderator's and participants' contributions, keeps track of speaking turns, records basic participation metrics, and uses that information to apply a fixed-rule algorithm to determine which participant speaks next. Participants (a set of persona agents participating in the focus group), and the Orchestrator (software to coordinate and record the interactions). Beyond this general architecture, it is worth clarifying how memory operates within a session, since it shapes what each agent can plausibly respond to. Participant agents do not have a separate memory store or private notes about the discussion. When called to speak, each participant receives its own prior response history together with the conversation that has occurred since it last spoke, rendered as plain transcript text.

In this sense, the participant's "memory" is not an independent record of the session, but the conversational context that is reintroduced at each turn.

The moderator has a different memory structure. It keeps a small set of running notes, updated after most turns. These notes track themes that have appeared, possible contradictions in participants' earlier statements, and whether the group is moving too quickly toward smooth consensus. The moderator's access to the transcript also depends on the structure of the discussion guide. Each guide section is treated as an active discussion block, defined by a main question and its sub-questions. While that block remains open, the moderator can see the full transcript of everything said within it, allowing it to decide whether to probe further, redirect the discussion, or move on.

When the system advances to the next section, the previous block is compressed into a short summary. From that point onward, the moderator no longer rereads the full transcript of the closed section, but relies on this summary as part of its memory of earlier discussion.

The participation algorithm seeks to operationalize the way in which turns can emerge in a group discussion. As illustrated in Figure 2, instead of assigning a fixed order, the system conducts an "auction" of turns: in each round, each participant privately evaluates (via their own API call) whether they want to speak based on the current context of the discussion (last 6 transcript entries) and assigns an urgency value between 0 and 1. To enter the auction, a participant must want to intervene and exceed the threshold of 0.55. If several participants exceed this threshold, the orchestrator selects the one with the highest urgency, with the tiebreaker favouring the agent who has spoken the least. The auction is modified to capture dynamics typical of a focus group. If someone is named by another participant, or if the moderator directs a question to several members, that person receives a limited bonus. However, if the moderator names a single participant, there is no auction: that person responds directly, simulating the moment when the group's attention shifts to the person who was addressed. Furthermore, if there is a high level of consensus, the system slightly favours those who wish to challenge the group; and if six turns pass without the moderator intervening, the system returns control to the moderator.

Synthetic agents

The starting point was the identification of datasets from human focus groups that could serve as a basis for comparison. After searching open repositories, 15 studies were identified. Of these, only five had discussion guides and verbatim transcripts available. Among these five cases, the composition of the focus groups and the availability of information about the participants were compared. Based on this review, Macho Meals (Hankins et al., 2025) was selected as the main case study, as it was the dataset that offered the greatest detail for constructing persona agents. It was decided to work with data linked to previously published studies not only because they had been collected by external researchers but also because they were accompanied by a prior analysis and findings that had been peer-reviewed as part of the academic publication process. This provided an initial reference regarding the expected themes and patterns in human groups, without that reference depending on the design of the present synthetic system.

Using the Macho Meals dataset (Hankins et al., 2025), a set of 22 persona agents was developed, corresponding to the male participants in the five focus groups from the original study. The participants ranged in age from 20 to 73 years, with a mean age of 43.1 years (SD = 15.8). This study, conducted in the UK, examined the relationship between the consumption of animal products and masculinity through a first quantitative phase and a second qualitative phase involving remotely moderated focus groups. This combination was useful for the simulation because the participants were linked not only to transcripts but also to individual metadata derived from the preliminary survey. For each participant, the following were recorded: pseudonym, age, gender, region, type of region, diet, scales related to masculinity and meat consumption, and frequency of consumption of red meat, chicken, fish, eggs, and dairy products. These data were used to construct the profiles without adding unobserved biographical details.

Design

The study employs a comparative focus group simulation design with experimental manipulation of the anchor level in the agents' profiles. To this end, the five Macho Meals focus groups were simulated three times each, maintaining the same participant composition as in the human reference group. These repetitions aim to mitigate the stochasticity inherent in LLM models, given that the inability to set a seed generates variability in responses to the same stimulus (Larooij & Törnberg, 2025). All sessions followed the original study's protocol, consisting of an introduction, five questions, and a conclusion. The analysis contrasts two conditions. In the basic condition, the agents are configured exclusively with demographic data. In the enriched condition, the agents incorporate all available metadata from the original study, which includes demographic information, dietary habits, and psychographic variables related to masculinity and meat consumption. This design allowed us to evaluate whether less detailed profiles can replicate human behaviour patterns with algorithmic fidelity equivalent to that of the more comprehensive profiles.

Accordingly, the study generated 30 synthetic focus-group sessions (5 focus groups × 2 conditions × 3 replications), alongside the five human sessions used as references (see Figure 3). The median execution time was 23.3 minutes per synthetic session, ranging from 13.1 to 42.2 minutes. The median cost was USD 2.54 per synth session, with individual sessions costing between USD 1.39 and USD 3.98, for a total cost of USD 75.38 across all 30 synthetic sessions.

Assessment benchmark

The evaluation benchmark consisted of 12 indicators, organized into three levels, designed to determine the extent to which synthetic focus groups replicate the properties of the human focus groups used as a reference. Given that focus group data are constructed in a situated and collective manner, the evaluation does not seek to verify whether the synthetic data meet a predefined quality standard, but rather to contrast them with human data: each indicator expresses a gap between the two, and it is the human transcripts that set the benchmark. The indicators were based on the differences documented in the literature between synthetic and human participants, for example, greater verbosity, homogenization of voices, less dissent, the moderator's prominence, or lower specificity, and by incorporating findings from previous studies on synthetic focus groups and the evaluation of persona agents (e.g. Zhang et al. (2024 2024)). It should be noted that the comparison was always made at the group, not participant, level. Although each human group had only one transcript, the five transcripts taken together show the extent to which the groups differ, and, when a metric allows for it, that variation becomes the criterion for evaluating the distance between a synthetic group and its human counterpart. Comparing each simulation with its own group and presenting the results group by group takes this limitation into account without eliminating it.

The first level, thematic fidelity, uses the codebook designed by the researchers in the original study (see Figure 4): a structured set of codes (labels of categories and themes with their definitions) that serves as a framework for classifying the content of the transcripts. Coding is performed by an evaluator LLM from a different family than the generator, blindly and identically on both sides, to avoid circularity between the evaluator (Gemini) and the generator (Claude). Before being used, the evaluator LLM must pass three quality control checks. Reproducibility checked whether the evaluator coded the same transcript identically across multiple iterations, to ensure that any differences observed between human and synthetic groups do not stem from variability within the LLM itself. Discrimination verified whether each human transcript achieves greater thematic overlap with its paired synthetic version than with synthetics from other groups, ensuring that the metric captures specific similarities rather than just general matches. Citation validity required that every coding decision be supported by a word-for-word verbatim confirmation in the transcript; any code without verifiable evidence was discarded, reducing the risk of citations fabricated by the LLM (for more detail see Appendix C). Beyond the first level of thematic fidelity, which focuses on content generation, the benchmark extends to two additional dimensions. The second level examined how the conversation unfolded, focusing on the length of turns and their distribution, how much that length varied from one focus group to another, the extent to which a turn raised and resolved conflicting positions on its own, and the density with which the discourse was anchored in specific contextual details. The third level, as a complementary analysis, addressed the distinguishability of speakers, that is, whether participants in the same session can be distinguished from one another and whether any of them maintain a recognizable way of speaking from one question to the next. Both properties are measured within each session by comparing participants with their own peers, and never by comparing a synthetic participant with the human whose profile was used to construct it. The resulting values at the group level were then compared across conditions. For details on each of the indicators, see Appendix D.

Results

Level 1. Thematic fidelity

The initial analyses were conducted to determine how well the two different groups of synthetic agents (basic vs. enriched) reproduced the themes present in the human data. The human focus groups produced a total of 11 different themes. In comparison, both sets of agents reproduced only part of the human repertoire, and the themes they repeated most consistently were not the human ones. Focus group discussion among the basic synths produced an average of 4.7 themes while the enriched synths covered 5.7 of them on average. In other words, the synthetic focus groups covered roughly half as many topics as their human counterparts.

The contrast was sharper for consistency. To illustrate this, Figure 5 maps exactly how many times each theme occurred (out of a maximum of 5) across the baseline and the six synthetic replications (3x basic and 3x enriched). Looking at the human column, two themes were present in all five groups: Nice and Not nice. The enriched replicates matched only the first, and only in two of the three replications, whereas the replications with basic synths matched neither. Not nice, the theme most robustly shared across the human groups, reached at most one of the five groups in any synthetic replicate. Conversely, Does influence was present in all five groups of every synthetic replicate, yet in only three of the five human groups. The agents were therefore most consistent about a theme on which the human participants were not, and least consistent about one on which they were. themes are shown along the left, colour coded by category. The first column shows the number of human focus groups (out of 5) that raised each theme. The next six columns report the number of synthetic focus groups (out of 5) that raised each theme. The cells' colour ranges from light (0) to dark (5) to visually illustrate the consistency effects.

Turning to theme saturation, Figure 6 tracks how quickly each study condition exhausted its own thematic repertoire. Rather than measuring against the full 11-theme human baseline, this analysis evaluates each replicate against its own final output to identify the exact point when new contributions ceased. The human baseline followed a common qualitative trajectory, generating most of its themes in the early sessions and reaching a stable levelling off after the third group. This is consistent with empirical evidence indicating that relatively homogenous human focus groups attached to narrow research objectives typically reach code saturation by the fourth group (Hennink et al., 2019).

The synthetic replications, however, diverged significantly from this expected human behaviour, displaying marked instability across runs. On one extreme, the basic synths occasionally exhibited premature saturation, exhausting its entirely limited repertoire as early as the first session (Basic Replication-2). On the other extreme, multiple synthetic runs continued to drip-feed single new themes up to the fifth group, failing to demonstrate a consistent levelling off at all. This erratic pattern demonstrates that while synthetic agents do accumulate themes, they fail to replicate the natural convergence and stabilization characteristic of human focus groups. saturation point is the last focus group that added a new codebook theme. "Not observed" indications that FG5 still added themes so no stable plateau was reached.

Shifting the focus away from complete replications, it is equally important to measure how accurately the models replicated specific, isolated conversations. To do this, we averaged the three synthetic runs for a given focus group, compared them to their direct human counterpart, and used three specific metrics. Recall captured the percentage of themes from a specific human group that its synthetic counterpart successfully managed to elicit. Precision looked at the other side of the equation, indicating how many of the themes generated by a synthetic group actually matched its specific human baseline. Finally, reach measured how widely a theme spread among the participants. For any theme that actually came up during a session, reach calculates the average percentage of participants who explicitly mentioned it, backed by a verified quote.

To illustrate these dynamics, Figure 7 plots the performance across all five sessions. In this graph, large markers represent the mean performance for a given condition, while the small open markers display the three individual runs, highlighting the natural variance in the models' outputs. When looking at the group-by-group averages (e.g. FG1 human vs. FG1 enriched), the enriched synths achieved a mean recall of 39.1%, while the basic synths trailed at 27.0%. Precision, however, remained strong across the board. The enriched groups saw 78.8% of their produced themes match the human data, and the basic groups reached 71.0%. What these values suggest is that while the simulations generated a narrower range of themes than the human baseline, the content they did manage to produce was largely accurate.

The differences between the conditions became much more pronounced when examining reach. In the enriched sessions, a given theme was expressed by an average of 77.1% of the participants. This represents an increase over both the human baseline (58.9%) and the basic sessions (65.4%). In other words, enriching the profiles pushed the synthetic participants to cluster more tightly around a shared set of themes. Notably, 44.6% of the enriched themes were voiced by every single group member. To put this in perspective, that level of full-group consensus only occurred for 14.9% of the themes in the human groups and 23.3% in the basic groups. In other words, the synth focus group discussions looked less like real people. They overstated how widely any given view was shared and lost the minority views and disagreement that real groups contained. Large markers show the mean of the three runs. Small markers show individual runs (R1-3). In the reach panel, diamonds show the paired human reference for each focus group.

Level 2. Interaction process

The greatest differences between human and synthetic groups occurred not in their thematic content, but in how the conversations actually unfolded. The most noticeable divergence was verbosity. Because turn lengths were strongly right-skewed, with a few exceptionally long interventions pulling up the arithmetic mean, central tendency was calculated as the median within each session and then averaged across sessions, giving each session equal weight.

On average, human participant turns (from when a participant began speaking until they finished or were interrupted) were concise: 43% contained 40 words or fewer and 41% ranged from 41 to 150 words, with a per-group median turn length averaging 49 words. To illustrate how these proportions compare across conditions, Figure 8 displays the full distribution of participant turn lengths. The simulations generated considerably longer responses, with 93% (basic) and 90% (enriched) of their turns spanning 151 to 400 words and group medians of roughly 240 words. The contrast is clearest among the shortest turns, with 34% of human turns falling below 25 words, whereas the shortest synthetic turn in the entire corpus of thirty sessions was 55 words. Moreover, human groups varied widely, with focus group medians ranging from 22 to 90 words with a coefficient of variation (CV, the percentage that the standard deviation represents relative to the mean) of 51.0%. In contrast, the synthetic conditions displayed uniformity across sessions since the equivalent between-group CV was 5.6% in the enriched condition and 6.6% in the basic condition. This shows that whereas human groups developed distinct conversational rhythms per group, the simulations applied a uniform output style regardless of group identity. That spread also puts the size of the gap in perspective. The largest difference between any two human focus groups is 68 words, and every one of the 30 synthetic sessions is further than that from its own human counterpart.

It was not possible to reliably determine the differences in the degree of consensus among participants of the different conditions. As exemplified in Figure 9, synthetic responses frequently combined acknowledgement, counterpoint and balance within a single turn. The pattern was first noticed while labelling the Level 1 analysis, and was then measured across all 779 participant-to-participant response mentions with a fixed list of contrastive expressions, resulting in 9.8% of synthetic mentions setting out two or more contrasting positions within the same turn, against 0.3% of human mentions. Rather than presenting a brief idea for another participant to challenge or build upon, the AI agents tended to anticipate alternative perspectives and resolve them internally before finishing the turn. Finally, to measure response specificity, references such as times, places, people, or food were counted. Because synthetic agents repeatedly name-dropped their assigned profiles (like London or Birmingham), geographic origins were excluded across all conditions. After this correction, human turns maintained a higher overall density of contextual references (3.17 per 100 words) than the basic (1.27) and enriched conditions (1.67), as shown in Figure 10. The sharpest gap appeared in references most closely related to the research topic of macho meals, named foods or dishes, where humans averaged 2.02 references per 100 words, compared to 0.89 in the enriched groups and just 0.24 in the basic groups. maximum across the five focus groups. The human data are the observed counts whereas the values for the Enriched and Basic groups are the mean over their three replications.

Level 3. Speaker distinctiveness

This final level evaluated whether participants maintained unique, recognizable identities rather than blending into a single generic voice. To test this, two complementary methods were applied to standardized-length text fragments extracted from identical questions across sessions: a predictive attribution test and a descriptive similarity measure.

First, an algorithm built a linguistic profile for each participant using a subset of questions and then tested whether it could correctly attribute an unseen fragment from a different question back to the correct individual. In the human groups, the task succeeded on 46.8% of attributions, against the 25.5% that random guessing would yield given the number of candidate speakers in each test. A permutation test confirmed this decisively exceeded chance (p < .001), and all five human sessions were individually above chance. The enriched condition performed no better than guessing with 32.5% against its own chance level of 31.2% (p = .34), and its sessions fell on either side of chance in equal measure. The basic condition barely exceeded chance, 37.7% hits against a chance level of 30.9% (p = .01), although the result was not corroborated when each session was treated as a single observation rather than pooling individual attributions across sessions.

Second, lexical similarity measured how far two participants' wording overlapped when both were answering the same focus group question. Comparing them on the same question holds the topic constant so what remains is how each person expresses their answer. Scores run from 0 (nothing in common) to 1 (identical). The medians were 0.179 in the human groups, 0.258 in the basic condition and 0.268 in the enriched one. Synthetic participants resembled one another roughly 45 to 50 per cent more than human participants did. The two analyses therefore converged: synthetic voices were less distinguishable and more homogeneous, with no clear advantage from enrichment.

Discussion

This study provides a new benchmark to evaluate the fidelity of LLM-generated focus groups, mapping how well they replicate both the thematic content and the interactive dynamics of human discourse. Rather than seeking a binary verdict on whether synthetic focus groups are 'faithful' to human counterparts, this research evaluates them across three distinct levels of performance to identify where simulations approximate human behaviour and where they diverge.

The results reveal that human-likeness depends both on the dimension being assessed and the research's intended use of synthetic focus groups. The synthetic focus groups tested captured a smaller, although largely plausible, set of the human themes raised in the conversation, and the enriched profiles improved this capture.

Nevertheless, while synthetic groups reproduced the substantive content of the discourse with some success, they did so with lower thematic consistency and missed subtle nuances, differing significantly in how participants socially structured their interactions, thus highlighting a core asymmetry between content fidelity and interactive organization This distinction is important because an incomplete thematic reconstruction does not necessarily invalidate the use of synthetic focus groups. For exploratory applications, such as testing a discussion guide, identifying candidate questions for further studies or anticipating possible lines of response, recovering a plausible subset of human themes may be sufficient. This interpretation is consistent with Novelli et al. (2026), who distinguish between instrumental uses of simulation and those in which interaction and the collective construction of meaning constitute the central object of interest.

Regarding thematic fidelity and alignment results, they indicate a bounded, rather than general, thematic alignment between humans and synths. The main problem was that the simulations retrieved only part of what appeared in the original groups and with different prevalence of each theme. This pattern is consistent with the findings of Amirova et al. (2024), who found considerable correspondence in the main beliefs expressed by human and synthetic participants, along with much more pronounced differences in their structure and tone. Zhang et al. (2024) Profile enrichment improved this reconstruction, but not without a cost. The enriched agents recovered more of the human repertoire than agents grounded only in demographic information, supporting the broader finding that richer empirical grounding can improve behavioural prediction (Park et al., 2024). Yet the themes that did emerge also spread across substantially more participants than in the human groups.

Enrichment therefore increased coverage while simultaneously concentrating the discussion around a narrower shared set of ideas. This is particularly important because additional persona information is commonly assumed to increase individual differentiation. Here, it did not simply make the agents "more human"; it changed which dimensions became collectively salient. Although the present design cannot establish the mechanism, this pattern is compatible with the focalism described by Toubia et al. (2025), whereby explicitly supplied attributes become disproportionately influential in LLM-generated behaviour.

The saturation results add a further consideration. Neither synthetic condition reproduced the human trajectory, in which most themes emerged early, and the repertoire stabilised after the third group. However, the two grounding approaches failed in different ways. The basic condition showed a greater tendency towards premature saturation, in the most extreme case exhausting its entire thematic repertoire after the first group. This reduces the marginal value of running additional focus groups as information can largely repeat, but in practice this is not a major problem since synthetic simulations are cheap and fast to run, unlike human fieldwork. The enriched condition, by contrast, continued to introduce new themes across later sessions.

Although this accumulation was more uneven than the human pattern and did not converge at the same point, richer grounding appeared to preserve some thematic yield from conducting multiple groups rather than collapsing immediately onto a fixed repertoire. Thus, enrichment did not reproduce human saturation, but it did make repeated synthetic sessions more informative.

The loss of themes or reduced prevalence of themes becomes particularly consequential when the purpose of the focus group is to capture the different facets of a phenomenon. The case of gender illustrates this clearly. At first glance, gender could appear to be a case of strong thematic fidelity: the idea that gender influences diet was among the most consistently reproduced themes in the synthetic groups. However, within the human groups, this position coexisted with its categorical denial and with the position described in the original study as 'No influence, but…', namely participants who consciously rejected the relevance of gender while describing strongly gendered dietary practices. The relationship between masculinity and diet therefore appeared, in some cases, to operate without a corresponding conscious articulation (Hankins et al., 2025).

The agents, on the other hand, tended to recognise and explicitly explain this relationship. The fact that this pattern also appeared in the exclusively sociodemographic condition suggests that it cannot be explained entirely by the psychographic information provided to the enriched profiles. One possible interpretation is that the model more readily reproduces available cultural knowledge about gender and diet than the resistance, contradiction or lack of awareness through which such knowledge may manifest itself in real individuals. This resembles the 'hyper-accuracy distortion' identified by Amirova et al. (2024), whereby an LLM response can be well-informed, coherent and objectively plausible while remaining less faithful to the perspective it is intended to represent.

In this case, the distortion can be understood as a form of interpretative overexplanation. The agents verbalised a relationship that some human participants appeared to reproduce without directly recognising it. The consequence is not simply that one position became more prevalent than another, but that part of the ambiguity surrounding the phenomenon was lost. This suggests that fidelity may be particularly difficult to achieve when the topic involves social desirability, identity, resistance or a gap between behaviour and self-perception. In such cases, a perfectly articulated response may in fact be less human. Fidelity therefore depends not only on recovering the ideas present in a population, but also on preserving their contradictions, implicitness and uneven articulation.

The difference became clearer when the analysis shifted from content to interaction. The synthetic turns were much longer, practically eliminated very short interventions, and showed considerably less direct continuity between participants than the human groups. These patterns persisted even after a comparison of prompt versions that substantially reduced verbosity, suggesting that they cannot be attributed to an initial, poorly calibrated version of the prompt alone.

Importantly, the additional length did not translate into greater contextual richness. Despite producing turns roughly five times longer at the median, both synthetic conditions contained fewer specific contextual references per 100 words than the human groups. Enrichment improved this dimension relative to basic grounding alone, suggesting that additional participant information helped anchor responses in more relevant detail. Yet it did not remove the broader interactional divergence: enriched and basic groups remained similarly verbose and displayed much less variation in conversational rhythm across sessions than humans. Profile enrichment therefore appears more effective at changing what information agents draw upon their profiles as anchors than at changing the underlying discourse form through which that information is expressed.

Agents also frequently acknowledged a previous contribution, introduced an alternative position and then qualified or reconciled it within the same response. This does not prove that there was either more consensus or more disagreement, but it does suggest that part of the deliberative process shifted from interaction between speakers to internal argumentation within the speaker. In a human conversation, a position can be formulated briefly and left open for another person to contradict, reformulate or expand upon. In the simulations, such alternative responses were more frequently anticipated by the agent themselves. In this sense, they resembled, in some respects, the logic of a group interview, while still retaining characteristics specific to a multi-agent conversation.

This difference may help to explain why previous synthetic conversations have shown high levels of agreement. Mator et al. (2025), for example, found that synthetic responses were more extensive and showed considerably greater convergence than those of human participants. The current results suggest that some of this overlap may not be explained by complacency alone. If several agents individually incorporate positions in favour, against and nuanced views, their responses will inevitably share more content, even if their final positions are not identical. The apparent harmony may therefore arise partly from redundant discursive coverage, rather than from an interpersonal process of consensus-building.

Finally, synthetic participants were more linguistically similar to one another and substantially harder to identify or differentiate from each other using their responses, compared to human participants with no clear improvement from profile enrichment. This suggests that providing agents with more individual information does not necessarily produce more individualised voices. Persona construction therefore involves two challenges, generating responses that are plausible given a profile, and maintaining a recognisable individual who expresses and prioritises that information in a distinctive way.

An important methodological consideration is that these divergences were observed in a system that sought to structure the conditions of the focus group without directly prescribing its behavioural outcomes. The architecture defined roles, conversational memory, participation mechanisms, access to the group context, moderation and progression through the guide, and explained to the agents what kind of interaction constituted a focus group. However, apart from general adjustments designed to discourage overly rehearsed responses, no fixed response lengths, predetermined percentages of disagreement, turn-taking distributions, specific linguistic styles or participant-to-participant interaction quotas were imposed. This was a deliberate decision. Introducing these properties directly might have produced conversations that were superficially more human-like, but it would have incorporated into the system some of the very behaviours subsequently used to assess its fidelity. For example, achieving turns of human-like length would be of little value as evidence if their length had been predetermined using the distribution observed in human transcripts. Instead, the design sought to provide the necessary scaffolding for a focus group interaction to emerge, rather than hard-coding the behaviours against which that interaction would subsequently be assessed. Under this logic, verbosity, the internalisation of contrast, or the reduced differentiation between voices are methodologically informative results precisely because they were not objectives programmed a priori. This distinction also addresses the need for transparency in social simulation highlighted by Dilaver and Gilbert (2023), particularly when interpreting emergent properties of the model.

Reducing stylistic hard-coding was also intended to avoid an architecture that was overly dependent on the specific characteristics of a single LLM. Different models may interpret very specific instructions regarding length, spontaneity or conversational style in different ways, therefore, exhaustively calibrating these characteristics for a specific model could reduce the system's portability or require re-engineering for each architecture. This does not imply that the system has been shown to be modelindependent (something which this study did not evaluate), but rather that it was designed so that the greater part of the specification relates to the conditions of interaction rather than to a manual imitation of the linguistic and behavioural surface of the human reference.

These results support a usage-dependent assessment, rather than a binary classification of synthetic focus groups as valid or invalid. For exploratory tasks, the advantages are significant. The low cost, speed and ability to repeatedly run the same configuration make it possible to test guidelines, trial analytical procedures, identify candidate themes and explore scenarios before investing in human fieldwork. The thematic accuracy observed suggests that these applications can produce plausible information, provided they are understood as exploratory input rather than a validated substitute for a human population. However, the standard must be different when the question depends on relative salience, the presence of minority opinions, resistance or the collective construction of meaning. Furthermore, the present results suggest that stability should be taken into account even within primarily thematic tasks: if a conclusion appears only in some runs, a single simulation does not allow us to determine whether a robust pattern or a favourable outcome has been identified.

In theoretical terms, the findings support the view that human-likeness should be understood as a multidimensional and situated property, rather than as a global attribute of a model. Evaluating synthetic focus groups using a single similarity indicator may, therefore, obscure precisely the dimension whose reproduction is central to their intended use.

The current findings rely on a specific case: a particular population, a single topic, a single generative model and a specific architecture. The results should not, therefore, be interpreted as universal properties of LLMs. The three-level benchmark proposed here, however, is independent of the details of this case. The benchmark allows us to assess the extent to which a textual, multi-agent architecture can approximate the observable functioning of a human focus group, even when the mechanisms governing conversation generation are not identical.

Beyond the performance of the simulations themselves, this study extends the emerging evidence on synthetic focus groups by evaluating their fidelity through several complementary dimensions within the same matched qualitative case. Rather than reducing human-likeness to a single outcome, the benchmark examines thematic correspondence, interactional process, and agent-level fidelity, while repeated simulations allow the stability of apparent correspondence to be considered across runs.

Previous studies have provided important evidence on different aspects of synthetic focus-group performance; the present benchmark brings several of these concerns together within a common evaluative framework. This makes it possible to examine not simply whether a simulation resembles its human reference, but which aspects are reproduced more closely, and which remain more difficult to approximate. Notably, Figure 10 reveals that while both synthetic conditions remain below human levels of detail, the Enriched synths fall entirely outside the human range in all cases. Conversely, the Basic synths, despite their overall lack of specificity, reach in two cases the lower bounds of the human range. This suggests that the models generally struggle to naturally weave in the personal experiences and habits that ground human discourse in lived discussions. The Enriched condition only outperforms the Basic one in the food-related category, likely because the explicit inclusion of dietary habits in their profiles provided the necessary cues for the model to generate those specific details. This indicates that without highly explicit prompts, the agents struggle to spontaneously pull from their persona data to anchor the conversation in the same way human participants do. simulation and evaluation code will be made publicly available at GitHub [https://github.com/LauraLP08/Human-Likeness-Benchmark-in-Synthetic-Focus-Groups], allowing the benchmark to be inspected, adapted, and tested with other populations, topics, models, and architectures.

Against this background of rapid, but unconsolidated progress, the general objective guiding this research aims to expand efforts to assess how reliably such systems can reproduce qualitative focus-group dynamics and, on that basis, how far their content approximates that of human groups in applied research settings. Consequently, the next step is to examine how this technical progress has been structured and what specific results have been presented in this area.

thematic relevance of the content, the pattern of code saturation across sessions, and the interactional character of the discussion. The first concerns whether the transcript covers the ideas and narratives needed to address the research objective. The second concerns whether additional sessions generate new codes, and whether human and synthetic focus groups show a comparable point at which thematic novelty begins to decline. The third concerns whether these themes emerge through recognisable group discussion. The literature offers clearer guidance for saturation than for the other levels, since there is no standard expectation that focus groups should contain a fixed number of disagreements, peer responses, or challenges per question. For this reason, the present study does not predefine what counts as a good discussion but uses the human transcripts as the reference point for comparison, asking whether synthetic groups reproduce similar patterns of discussion. The indicators developed in the methodology are therefore intended as a pragmatic way to compare human and synthetic focus groups, rather than as general measures of focus group quality.
